problem: Sessions 114-118 got you to a genuinely solid single-host Docker workflow: containers built, networked, storing data safely, hardened, and versioned with a real promotion path. But every one of those sessions assumed one host. The moment ethics-triage, its database, and its API need to survive a host reboot, scale beyond what one machine can handle, or keep running when a server dies at 2am, 'one host running docker run' stops being enough — nothing restarts a crashed container automatically, nothing moves a container to a healthy machine if the one it's on fails, and nothing coordinates rolling out a new version across multiple machines without downtime.

This is the exact gap Kubernetes closes: it takes everything from Sessions 114-118 (images, networking, storage, security, versioned tags) and adds a layer that decides which of many machines runs which containers, keeps them running, and reacts automatically when something goes wrong.
concept: Kubernetes (K8s) is a container orchestrator: given a cluster of machines and a description of what you want running, it schedules containers onto machines, restarts them if they crash, replaces them if a machine dies, and can scale the number of running copies up or down — all continuously, without you manually running docker run anywhere.

The core idea is declarative, not imperative: instead of issuing commands ('start this container'), you describe a desired state ('I want 3 copies of ethics-api always running'), and a set of control loops continuously work to make reality match that description.

Object What it represents Pod The smallest deployable unit — one or more tightly- coupled containers sharing network/storage Deployment Declares how many replicas of a Pod should run, and how to roll out updates Service A stable network identity/IP for a set of Pods, even as individual Pods come and go Node A physical or virtual machine in the cluster that actually runs Pods Namespace A way to partition a cluster into isolated groups of resources
deep: The control loop — Kubernetes' core mechanism Every Kubernetes object has a desired state (what you declared) and a status (what's actually true right now). A continuous reconciliation loop compares the two and takes action to close any gap — if a Deployment declares 3 replicas and only 2 Pods are running, the loop creates a new one; if 4 are running, it deletes one. This single mechanism, repeated for every object type, is what makes Kubernetes self-healing.

Cluster architecture: control plane and nodes Component Role API server The front door — every kubectl command and every internal component talks through it etcd The cluster's database — stores all desired-state and current-state data Scheduler Decides which node a new Pod should run on, based on resources and constraints Controller manager Runs the reconciliation loops (Deployments, ReplicaSets, etc.)

kubelet (on each node) The agent that actually starts/stops containers via the container runtime kube-proxy (on each node) Implements Service networking rules on each node Pods — why not just containers A Pod wraps one or more containers that must be scheduled together, share a network namespace (so they can reach each other via localhost), and share storage volumes. Most Pods run exactly one container; multi-container Pods exist for tightly coupled helper patterns (a sidecar that ships logs from the main container, for example).
- name: ethics-api image: registry/ethics-api:1.4.2 # Session 118's tag discipline ports:

limits: { memory: "256Mi", cpu: "500m" } Services — stable addressing for Pods that come and go Pods are ephemeral and get new IPs when recreated. A Service gives a stable DNS name and virtual IP in front of a group of Pods (selected by label), and kube-proxy load-balances traffic across whichever Pods currently match — the cluster-scale equivalent of the container-name DNS resolution from Session 115.
workflow: Applied as the natural next step for the ethics-triage/ethics-api/ethics-db stack from Sessions 115-118, once it's outgrown a single host:
1. Write a Deployment manifest for ethics-api referencing the exact versioned image tag from Session 118's promotion workflow — never latest.
2. Write a Service manifest exposing ethics-api internally, and a separate Service (or Ingress) exposing it externally — mirroring the 'one published entry point' pattern from Session 115.
3. Write a StatefulSet (not a plain Deployment) for ethics-db, paired with a PersistentVolumeClaim — the cluster-scale evolution of the named volume from Session 116.
4. Apply everything: kubectl apply -f ., and let the control loop reconcile the cluster to match.
5. Watch Kubernetes handle failure: kill a Pod manually (kubectl delete pod <name>) and observe the Deployment's control loop create a replacement automatically within seconds.
6. Roll out a new version by changing only the image tag in the Deployment manifest and reapplying — Kubernetes performs a rolling update, replacing Pods gradually with zero downtime.
enterprise: Kubernetes sits directly on top of everything from Layer 8's earlier sessions and is usually the point where 'containers' stops being an individual engineer's tool and becomes shared, managed infrastructure with its own team or platform group.

Layer Role Application containers The images from Sessions 114-118, unchanged Kubernetes cluster Schedules, heals, scales, and network-routes those containers across many nodes Platform/infra team Owns cluster health, upgrades, and shared policies (Session 117's hardening enforced cluster-wide) Application teams Own their Deployment/Service manifests, deploying into a cluster they don't operate directly This split — infra owns the cluster, application teams own what runs on it — is exactly the kind of role separation your own trajectory (support/ops moving toward infrastructure) is aimed at eventually sitting on the infra side of.
dependencies: A container runtime on every node (containerd, the same one underlying Docker — Session 114) to actually start containers.
Networking (Session 115's concepts, implemented cluster-wide via a CNI plugin like Calico or Cilium) so Pods on different nodes can reach each other.
Persistent storage backends (Session 116's concepts, implemented via cloud block storage or NFS) so PersistentVolumes can follow a rescheduled Pod to a different node.
etcd, a distributed key-value store, as the cluster's single source of truth for all state.
Container images built, scanned, and tagged per Sessions 114, 117, and 118 — Kubernetes schedules images, it doesn't build or secure them.
dependents: Helm (Session 120, next) — a package manager for Kubernetes manifests, letting complex multi- object applications be templated and versioned as one unit.
Service Mesh (Session 121) — adds fine-grained traffic control, mTLS between services, and observability on top of the basic Service networking described here.
Horizontal Pod Autoscaling and cluster autoscaling — both depend entirely on the reconciliation- loop mechanism explained in Deep Tech.
Most modern CI/CD pipelines' final deploy step, which is typically kubectl apply or a GitOps tool syncing manifests into a cluster.
security: Risk Mitigation Overly permissive default namespace access Use namespaces to isolate teams/apps; apply RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) per namespace Pods running with container-level risks from Session 117 unchecked cluster-wide Pod Security Standards / admission controllers enforce non-root, no --privileged, etc. at the cluster level Unrestricted Pod-to-Pod network traffic NetworkPolicies — the Kubernetes-native version of Session 115's 'segment by trust boundary' Secrets stored in plain manifests Use Kubernetes Secrets (still base64, not encrypted, by default) combined with an external secrets manager for anything sensitive Risk Mitigation Unpatched, unscanned images still running Admission controllers can block images that fail Session 117's scanning gate from ever being scheduled The scale-up of a familiar idea Every security control from Session 117 still applies — Kubernetes doesn't replace container hardening, it just gives you a cluster-wide way to enforce it consistently instead of trusting every engineer to remember it per container.
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Cause First Command Pod stuck in Pending Insufficient node resources, or unsatisfiable scheduling constraints kubectl describe pod <name> Pod in CrashLoopBackOff Container exits immediately on start (same root causes as Session 114) kubectl logs <pod> -- previous Service has no endpoints Label selector doesn't match any running Pods kubectl get endpoints <service> Rolling update stuck mid-rollout New Pods failing readiness probes kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> Can't reach a Service from outside the cluster No Ingress/LoadBalancer configured, or misconfigured kubectl get svc,ingress Pod evicted unexpectedly Node under memory/disk pressure, or resource limits exceeded kubectl describe node <node> kubectl describe <object> is the single most useful troubleshooting command in Kubernetes — it shows recent Events for that object, which almost always names the actual problem (failed scheduling, failed pulls, failed health checks) in plain language.
example: A realistic trajectory for the CEx tooling stack, once it's outgrown a single VM: ethics-api and ethics- triage run as Deployments with multiple replicas for availability, ethics-db runs as a StatefulSet (or, more likely in practice, is replaced by a managed Cloud SQL instance per Session 116's cloud-perspective guidance), and a rolling deploy of a bug fix to ethics-api happens with zero downtime — old Pods keep serving traffic while new ones spin up and pass health checks, and only then are old ones terminated.

Pattern to notice The database is usually the piece enterprises pull OUT of Kubernetes and into a managed service, even as everything else moves in — Session 116's storage caveats about containerized databases only get stronger at cluster scale, where a Pod can be rescheduled to a completely different physical machine.
cloud: Running Kubernetes yourself (self-managed control plane) is a significant operational burden; every major cloud provider offers a managed control plane instead, which is how the overwhelming majority of real-world Kubernetes actually runs.

Provider Managed service What's managed for you Google Cloud GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine) Control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler) fully managed; you manage nodes (or use Autopilot for that too) AWS EKS Control plane managed; node groups still your responsibility unless using Fargate Azure AKS Same pattern — managed control plane, self-managed or managed node pools Given CEx's existing Google-based stack, GKE (particularly GKE Autopilot, which also manages node infrastructure) is the natural landing spot if tooling ever grows to genuinely need orchestration — though it's worth being honest that Cloud Run (Session 116/118's cloud perspective) is the right choice for far longer than most teams assume, since it gives most of Kubernetes' self-healing and scaling benefits with none of the cluster-operations overhead.
automation: Manifests are declarative YAML, which means they belong in Git exactly like application code — this is the foundation of GitOps, where the cluster's actual state is continuously reconciled to match what's committed to a repository, rather than deployed by a person running commands.

# Conceptual CI/CD deploy step, extending Session 118's promotion flow - name: Update image tag in manifest run: | sed -i "s|image:.*|image: registry/ethics-api:${{ github.sha }}|" \ k8s/deployment.yaml - name: Apply to cluster run: kubectl apply -f k8s/ - name: Wait for rollout to succeed run: kubectl rollout status deployment/ethics-api The rollout status check is what makes this safe to automate: if the new version's Pods fail their health checks, the pipeline fails loudly instead of silently leaving a broken rollout half-finished.
career: Kubernetes is close to the single most in-demand infrastructure skill in job postings today, and it's also one of the most commonly overclaimed — a lot of candidates can recite Pod/Deployment/Service definitions without having debugged a real CrashLoopBackOff or a stuck rollout. Having done the lab below, with real failure and recovery, is a meaningfully stronger interview answer than reciting the object model.

For your trajectory specifically, Kubernetes is the natural ceiling of the container arc that started with Docker in Session 114 — being able to speak concretely about the progression from 'one container on my laptop' to 'a self-healing, auto-scaling cluster' is exactly the kind of narrative arc that makes a self- taught infrastructure background credible to a hiring manager.
interview: 7. What's the difference between a Pod, a Deployment, and a Service?
8. Explain, at a mechanical level, how Kubernetes' reconciliation loop keeps the actual state matching the desired state.
9. How does Kubernetes perform a rolling update, and what makes it zero-downtime?
10. A Pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff — walk through how you'd debug it.
11. Why might a team choose a managed database service over running a database as a StatefulSet in Kubernetes?
12. What's the role of etcd in a Kubernetes cluster, and what happens if it becomes unavailable?
13. How do NetworkPolicies relate to the container-networking segmentation concepts from earlier sessions?
misconceptions: Misconception Reality Kubernetes replaces Docker It orchestrates containers; the images are still built with Docker (or another OCI-compatible builder) exactly as in Session 114 A Pod is the same thing as a container A Pod wraps one or more containers with shared network/storage; most wrap exactly one, but they're not synonyms Kubernetes automatically makes an application secure It gives you the mechanisms (RBAC, NetworkPolicies, Pod Security Standards); you still have to configure them Misconception Reality Deleting a Pod is dangerous For a Pod managed by a Deployment, it's routine — the control loop replaces it immediately, often used deliberately to test resilience You always need Kubernetes once you have multiple containers docker-compose is entirely sufficient for many single- host, multi-container needs; Kubernetes solves multi- host, self-healing, and scaling problems specifically
anchors: Deployment says 'I want 3.' The control loop is the relentless assistant that keeps making that true, forever, without being asked twice.
Pod = the shipping container. Node = the ship it rides on. Kubernetes = the port authority deciding which ship carries which container, and replacing a lost container automatically.
Service = a phone number that always reaches 'customer support,' even though the specific agent (Pod) answering changes constantly.
kubectl describe = 'what happened here, in plain language' — the first command for nearly every problem.
connections: This session is the payoff of the entire Docker arc (Sessions 114-118), scaled from one host to a cluster:
Session 114 (Docker): Kubernetes schedules and runs the exact same images, via the same container runtime concepts, just across many nodes instead of one.
Session 115 (Container Networking): Services and NetworkPolicies are the direct cluster-scale evolution of Docker's bridge networks and 'only publish what must be reached.'
Session 116 (Container Storage): PersistentVolumes/PersistentVolumeClaims are the cluster-scale evolution of named volumes, solving the added problem of storage following a Pod across nodes.
Session 117 (Container Security): Pod Security Standards and NetworkPolicies enforce the same non-root/capability/segmentation practices cluster-wide instead of per-container.
Session 118 (Image Lifecycle): rolling updates depend entirely on deploying by specific, immutable tag — deploying 'latest' into a Deployment defeats rollback exactly as it did in Session 118.
Availability as a built-in, automated property of the platform rather than a manually engineered pattern.

Forward-looking: Session 120 (Helm) packages the manifests introduced here into reusable, versioned templates. Session 121 (Service Mesh) adds traffic control and encryption on top of the Service networking covered here.

lab: Hands-on: deploy the ethics-api container from earlier sessions onto a local Kubernetes cluster and put the self-healing behavior to the test.
14. Install a local single-node cluster: minikube start (or enable Kubernetes in Docker Desktop).
15. Write deployment.yaml declaring 3 replicas of your ethics-api image (use the versioned tag from Session 118's lab, not latest).
16. Write service.yaml exposing it, type: LoadBalancer (minikube service ethics-api will give you a reachable URL).
17. Apply both: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml -f service.yaml, then kubectl get pods -w and watch all 3 come up.
18. Test self-healing: kubectl delete pod <one-of-the-three> and watch a replacement appear automatically within seconds — note the new Pod's different name/IP but identical behavior.

19. Test a rolling update: change the image tag in deployment.yaml to a new version, kubectl apply again, and watch kubectl rollout status deployment/ethics-api — confirm the Service stayed reachable throughout.

20. Deliberately break it: set the image tag to something nonexistent, apply, and use kubectl describe pod on the resulting Pod to find the exact error message Kubernetes reports for a failed image pull.
21. Clean up: kubectl delete -f . and minikube stop.

Production tie-in Steps 5 and 6 are the two behaviors that justify Kubernetes' operational complexity — automatic recovery from a crashed Pod, and a rollout that never takes the whole service offline. If a workload doesn't need either, Sessions 114-118's single-host approach is often the better, simpler choice.
notes: Space for your own observations after completing the lab — what surprised you about how fast self- healing kicked in, anything about the rollout that behaved differently than expected, and questions to carry into Session 120 (Helm).
